notes.note.john-hours: John's hours are debated. Most readers count from sunrise (so the sixth hour is about noon), but some think John uses the Roman civil day counted from midnight, which would move the time of day.
notes.note.long-cubit: Ezekiel's temple vision is measured in a longer cubit: the common cubit plus a handbreadth, as this verse says. That is about 52 cm instead of about 46 cm, and it applies to every cubit in chapters 40 to 48.
notes.note.roman-watches: Jesus names the four watches of the Roman night: evening, midnight, cockcrow and morning. The Old Testament knew three night watches, not four.
notes.note.stature-cubit: A cubit (about 45 cm) is a real measure, used here as an example of a small amount; the exact length is not the point. The Greek word for stature can also mean length of life.
notes.v.14003003: 'After the first measure' most likely points to the older, longer cubit standard rather than a later, shorter one, so these cubits are counted as long cubits.
notes.v.40018024: Ten thousand talents is an unpayable sum, many lifetimes of a labourer's wages. The size of the debt is the point of the parable.
notes.v.40020002: A denarius was the usual day's pay for a labourer, so the owner is offering the ordinary daily wage. The same coin comes back in verses 9, 10 and 13.
notes.v.41015025: Counted from sunrise, the third hour is about 9 a.m. Compare John 19:14, where the sixth hour is disputed.
notes.v.43019014: The 'sixth hour' is disputed. Counted from sunrise it is about noon; counted from midnight in the Roman civil way it is about 6 a.m. Mark 15:25 puts the crucifixion at the third hour, about 9 a.m. by sunrise counting.
notes.v.44023023: 'The third hour of the night' counts hours of darkness from sunset, about 6 p.m., so this is roughly 8 to 9 p.m. It is not the third hour of the day (about 9 a.m.).
